doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Meeting Goodman, Ramapo workshop and teaching himself tenor sax
summary: Getting Goodman's autograph, the Ramapo jazz workshop faculty, and self-teaching tenor from a Lester Young solo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: know I said oh my God, you know. He went, “Well would you like to come with me.” “Would I like to come with you?” But then how am I going to — my father is going to have to drive back and leave me for three or four hours and then either go back to Fairlawn or go sit somewhere, and I went with Teddy Wilson and I got autographs. It was Lionel Hampton, Gene Krupa, Benny Goodman, Lionel Hampton, Illinois Jacquet played with them, and I think it was George Duvivier or Slam Stewart. And I got all these autographs. And that was the first time that I met Goodman and then when he came to the Jazz Museum I said well I had got your autograph, as though he would remember you know. And he said well maybe you want to come — and I wanted an autographed picture. He said, “Well call my office.” So I called his office and it was on a weekend or something, I went in and it was a woman named Muriel Zuckerman, who had been Benny Goodman’s personal aide for 40 years, like a real Girl Friday kind of thing. She was in love with the boss and a wonderful woman. And I went in and I got this autograph of Benny Goodman, little did I know that I would be running that office several years later. So this is all just giving context to what happened to me before I went to college. Then also in New Jersey there was a jazz workshop at a place called Ramapo College. And it was one of the first I think serious like jazz like summer jazz workshop kind of thing for kids. This was in the early 70s, mid 70s. And it was run by a man named Harold Lieberman, a wonderful trumpet player. He did some studio work. And he had an assistant working for him by the name of Dick Lowenthal. And so they had this wonderful program. And among the faculty were Frankie Dunlop, the drummer who played with Thelonious Monk, Bucky Pizzarelli, Derek Smith, and oh man there was someone else who I just am blanking on, Paul Jeffrey, the saxophone player. And Kenny Washington, I met him there, he was on this thing. And so I was very lucky, when I said about luck, you know because at that time kind of like a burgeoning of jazz education for kids, the Jazz Museum happened to start in New York, Teddy Wilson happened to have a weekend off from playing in Hackensack, New Jersey, and all these things are just coming together. Well I fell in love with the Benny Goodman record at Carnegie Hall, and for whatever reason I zeroed in on this tenor sax solo that Lester Young played on that concert. And I had taken a couple of clarinet lessons, never got very far on it, but at least I learned the fingering. And there was a tenor sax in the high school band room. And I kind of taught myself to play it. I mean it’s not hard to teach yourself the saxophone if you’ve taken a couple of clarinet lessons. I mean it’s very simple fingering and much simpler than the clarinet.
And so I picked it up and slowly began this move towards not focusing exclusively on the piano but starting to play the saxophone. So that all happened at that time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
